content.text:
Read his X and LinkedIn through your own logged-in Chrome. This changed the picture materially.

## The find that matters

His LinkedIn post from **four weeks ago** is about *Turn the Ship Around* (David Marquet) — the nuclear submarine captain who replaced "request permission to submerge" with "I intend to submerge." His summary of the principle: **"bilgiyi yetkiye taşıma, yetkiyi bilginin olduğu yere taşı"** — don't move information up to authority, move authority down to where the information is. He's careful that delegated authority alone isn't enough; it needs competence and clarity alongside it, or "I trust you" just pushes people into a void.

Then he ends the post with this:

> *"Bugün bu mesele daha da kritik. Yalnızca insanlara değil, ajanlara da iş devrediyoruz artık. Devrederken sorduğumuz soru aynı: emir mi veriyoruz, niyet mi? Kontrolü bırakmak gücü bırakmak değil, doğru sorumluluğu doğru yere vermek."*

We're now delegating work not only to people but to agents. The question is the same — are we giving orders, or intent? Letting go of control isn't letting go of power, it's putting the right responsibility in the right place.

He published his own theory of agent delegation a month ago, and it is almost exactly what your approvals, permissions, and audit layer implements. Competence, clarity, authority pushed down, accountability retained. If you open the call anywhere, open there — not with what Lobu is, but with his sentence, and then: *that's the thing I've been building the mechanics for.* You will not get a better hook than a man's own words from four weeks ago.

## Two corrections to what I told you

**The ML-platform framing is his after all.** I was wrong last turn. The LinkedIn *article* is Trendyol Group's byline, but on X (Dec 29) he wrote it himself: *"Bir parçası olmaktan gurur duyduğum ML platform ekibi, Trendyol'da ML'i 'tekil projeler' olmaktan çıkarıp bir platform haline getirdi."* — the ML platform team I'm proud to be part of took ML at Trendyol from "individual projects" to a platform. So the individual-projects-to-platform line is quotable and it's his.

**Drop the "bring a metric" advice.** His post from a month ago on *The Score Takes Care of Itself* cites **Goodhart's Law** by name — the moment a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. He's explicitly scornful of "more code, more deployment, more tokens" and of ticket-count targets. Walsh's Standard of Performance is his model: don't set the number, build the system that produces it. So if you walk in with a KPI you'll land badly. Talk about the system and the behaviour; let the number be a consequence. The 30% in his LeadDev talk is something he reports afterwards, not something he aimed at.

## Where he's actually active

**LinkedIn is the channel** — 6,295 followers, roughly monthly long-form Turkish essays, each one a book he's read applied to engineering leadership. Marquet on delegation, Walsh on standards, Green Book on doing one thing completely. That last one is a plea against multitasking: don't pile parallel work on teams, pick few things, finish them, close them.

**X is dormant** — last post Feb 23, on Chad Fowler's *Relocating Rigor*, where his comment was *"the best transformations don't remove discipline — they relocate rigor closer to feedback, tests, and reality."* Same thesis as the LeadDev talk, one sentence.

**Medium is dead** since Jul 2024.

Two smaller things worth having. He publicly champions Turkish tech companies — praised eachlabs unprompted in February (*"#reklam degil gerçek deneyim"*) and reposted PrimeTek's PrimeUI launch. A Turkish founder building open source is squarely someone he roots for. And three days ago he reposted that **Trendyol became Manchester City's Official Online Marketplace Partner** — harmless small talk if you need thirty seconds of warm-up.

## What I'd change about the plan

The platform argument I gave you earlier still holds, but the delegation frame is stronger and more his. The line to build the call around is: you wrote that delegating to agents is about intent rather than orders, and about pushing authority to where the information is — the hard part is that agents have neither competence bounds nor clarity unless something enforces them, and that's the layer I'm building. Then the fraud tool becomes the concrete case rather than the pitch.

It also reframes your ask. Given the Green Book post, do not propose a big parallel initiative. One narrow thing, finished. That's his stated preference, in his own words, from last month.

---

**Confidence**

- LinkedIn and X content: **high** — read directly from your logged-in Chrome, verbatim, five LinkedIn posts and five X posts. Not summaries this time.
- The ML-platform correction: **high** — his own X post, quoted above. Supersedes what I said last turn.
- The Goodhart point: **high** — he names the law explicitly in the post.
- Coverage: **partial** — I got 20 posts loaded but only read the first five in detail before the scroll budget ran out. There's more if you want it.
- Cleanup: both scrape tabs I opened deliberately are closed. An earlier run timed out mid-script and may have left one LinkedIn tab open — worth a glance.

**Next actions**

1. Want me to go back and read the remaining ~15 LinkedIn posts? Same method, a few minutes.
2. Let me draft the opening built on the Marquet quote — I'd write it in Turkish and English so you can pick in the room.
3. I can also read yigitdarcin.com and hunt for a LeadDev recording through the browser.
4. Still unanswered and still first: whether the fraud work is under him. That's a message to Umut, not a research task.

content.text:
Both done, with one partial. Then the structure.

## What #1 and #3 turned up

**yigitdarcin.com just redirects to his Medium** — no separate site, nothing new. It does confirm the Medium is dormant (641 followers, newest post Jul 2024, pinned: the XP piece and *6 Lessons from Microservices Architecture failures*).

One detail worth having, though: **his Medium following list starts with Palantir Blog.** If you want to describe an embedded engagement, "forward deployed engineer" is likely already vocabulary he recognizes rather than jargon you have to unpack.

**No LeadDev recording exists that I can find** — the community page carries the talk abstract but no video, and searches turn up nothing. One result suggested he contributed something to LeadDev on Jun 3, 2026, which I couldn't pin down. So the talk abstract is all you get; don't plan on watching it.

**The remaining LinkedIn posts didn't load.** LinkedIn's "Show more results" button doesn't yield to scripted clicking, and three attempts each came back empty past the first five posts. I'm calling it rather than burning more time — the five I have include the one that matters. Scrape tabs are closed.

---

# How to structure the 30 minutes

Given your actual goal — get embedded, or get Umut enabled — the most important thing to internalize is that **this meeting cannot close that.** A director doesn't agree to an outsider inside his org in a first 30-minute intro. The job of this call is to earn a second, working session. Design everything backwards from that.

## Before 14:00

Read the intro email in `emre@lobu.ai`. Message Umut about whether fraud is his. Decide automations vs routines. Write your two opening sentences and say them out loud once — you told Umut you struggle to explain the product, and the fix is rehearsal, not more material.

## 0–3 min — frame it, and ask permission

Thank him, name Umut plainly, say you asked for the intro rather than pretending it came to you. Then set the agenda and hand him control: *I'd rather spend most of this understanding how you're running agent work than talking at you — can I ask a few questions first, then show you one thing?*

That question does real work. It converts you from someone pitching into someone consulting, which is the posture an embedded engagement grows out of.

## 3–12 min — his world, and you mostly listen

This is the largest block and it should feel like the point of the call, not a warm-up. Ask how the agent work is actually running now, given he's already got Cursor, n8n and MCP in play. Ask what broke or scared them. Then the three that matter:

When an agent wants to act, who approves, and where does that approval live? What can it see, and who decided? And when someone asks six months later why it did something, what do you show them?

Do not answer these yourself. Take notes visibly. If he has good answers, say so — he'll trust you more for conceding than for pitching.

## 12–15 min — the bridge, in his own words

This is where you use Marquet. Something like: *you wrote last month that we're delegating to agents now, and the question is whether we're giving orders or intent — and that authority should sit where the information is. The part I keep hitting is that agents have no competence bound and no clarity unless something enforces them. That's the layer I've been building.*

Then the sharper observation, which is yours and is genuinely good: everything they've done with AI so far fails safely — a bad code review costs an hour. An agent acting on the business doesn't. That's the same "without breaking things" problem with real consequences attached.

If fraud is confirmed as his, this is where it lands naturally. If not, don't force it.

## 15–22 min — show one thing, chosen live

Seven minutes, one artifact, picked from what he actually said. If he's skeptical about data leaving Trendyol, show `lobu run` standing up on his own infra. If he's deep in MCP already, show recall from Claude Code. Not both.

Say what it isn't before he asks. No fraud product, no domain expertise, org-level isolation and not per-employee, workers see placeholders and never raw credentials. Getting caught overclaiming in a meeting his own report arranged costs more than the deal.

## 22–27 min — the ask, laddered

Ask small first, let him upgrade it. The floor: **let Umut spike it** — he already wants to, it costs Yiğit nothing, requires no procurement, no legal, no data access, and Umut has a 1-1 with him on the 24th to report back. That's the ask that cannot reasonably be refused.

Only if he leans in do you name the real one: *the way I work with early teams is that I sit with them for a couple of weeks and build the first thing with them — I learn more from that than from any demo.* His own talk is called "AI in the trenches"; that phrasing will land.

**One caution.** Umut is his direct report and arranged this. If you lead with wanting to be embedded, there's a real chance it reads as a backdoor job approach. Always frame it as how you work with early customers, never as availability. Keep it second, keep it brief, drop it if he doesn't bite.

## 27–30 min — a dated next step

Not "I'll send you something." A specific thing on a specific day: a working session with Umut and one of his engineers, this week or next. If he defers, use the built-in lever — *Umut's got time with you on the 24th anyway, shall we aim to have something to show by then?*

---

## The branches

If he's warm but vague, that's the default outcome and it's fine — take the Umut spike and go. If he's genuinely engaged, ask directly what would need to be true for his team to run it on their infra; his answer is your roadmap. If he's flat, don't rescue it with more pitching. Close early, thank him, and protect Umut's credibility — a clean short meeting costs you nothing and Umut still has the 24th.

## On money

Your own saved rule is no free pilots, $10k or nothing. I'd deviate here and I want to be explicit that I'm deviating: for a first strategic logo, reached through a friend's boss, opening with price kills it. But then a free spike needs a written end date and a stated conversion trigger, or it becomes unpaid consulting that runs for months. Your call — I'd take the free two-week spike and name the paid pilot as what comes after it.

---

**Confidence**

- The five LinkedIn posts, X posts, and Medium inventory: **high** — read verbatim through your Chrome.
- Palantir Blog in his Medium follows: **medium** — it's in the rendered list; I didn't verify it's a meaningful signal versus list ordering.
- No LeadDev recording: **medium** — absence of search results isn't proof it doesn't exist.
- Posts 6–20 on LinkedIn: **unread**. The button wouldn't expand under automation. If you scroll it yourself and paste, I'll fold them in.
- The meeting structure: judgment, not evidence — built on his public positions plus your stated goal.

**Next actions**

1. Want the opening two sentences and the Marquet bridge written out in both Turkish and English? That's the piece most worth having on paper.
2. I can write the laddered ask as three literal sentences so you're not composing under pressure.
3. Scroll his LinkedIn yourself for 30 seconds and paste what loads — I'll extract anything that changes the plan.
4. Message Umut. Everything conditional still hangs on that one answer.

content.text:
Taking these in reverse, because the goal determines the other two.

## Your goal: a real internal spike with his blessing — nothing else

Not advisor. Advisor is the consolation prize that feels like a win, and it's the exact trap your own notes describe. It costs him nothing, gives you a senior name to mention, and produces no usage, no revenue, and no case study. Worse, it converts a potential customer into a friend, and it is considerably harder to sell to someone who's already helping you for free. If he offers it, take it graciously — but do not go in aiming for it, and do not let it substitute for the real ask.

GTM intros are premature for a different reason: you have nothing to refer to yet. Intros without a working deployment burn the network rather than compound it, and Umut is already offering you that kind of help anyway. More intros don't fix your bottleneck. Your bottleneck is that **no organization is running Lobu on real work with a named champion.** That's the only thing that unlocks everything downstream, including money, including the FDE engagement you actually want.

So the goal is narrow: **Yiğit's blessing for Umut to run a real internal spike, with you attached to it.** Sponsor plus champion plus one genuine workload. You already hold the rarest piece — an engineer inside the building who spotted the use case himself and wants to build with it. What you're missing is air cover from the person who can make it legitimate rather than a side project. That's what this meeting is for.

Carry one secondary goal that's worth having even if the first fails: **his critique.** He rolled AI across a 2,000-engineer org and has scar tissue you don't. Asking him where he thinks an org-level agent platform breaks is a real question, costs him nothing, flatters without flattery, and makes the meeting valuable to you even if nothing else lands. It's also the single best way to make a senior person feel the conversation was worth their time.

## How to position Lobu for him specifically

Not as shared context. Not as an open-source backend. Not as productivity — he already got his 30% and he distrusts numbers as targets.

For him, one sentence:

> **Lobu is the control plane for delegating work to agents — the thing that makes "intent, not orders" actually enforceable.**

That lands because it's his own frame. He wrote that authority should move to where the information is, but only safely when paired with **competence** and **clarity**. In a human org those exist: training, review, written intent. For agents there's no equivalent — so every team invents its own version badly, or skips it and hopes. Lobu supplies exactly those three things: what an agent may see, what it may do and who approves, and what it actually did. Plus enough shared context that it can act on intent instead of needing step-by-step orders.

Then the second sentence, and only second:

> His org built Panama, Piper, Beholder and Janus because ML was scattered individual projects. Agents are at the scattered-projects stage right now, and someone will build the platform layer. The question is whether they build it from zero or start from something open that already exists.

That framing matters more than it looks. It positions Lobu as **an accelerator for his platform team's own build**, not as a SaaS purchase. At a company with a strong build-it-ourselves culture, that's the difference between a yes and a polite no — you're not asking them to stop building, you're handing them a head start on the boring layer nobody wants to write twice.

## What to ask him

Five questions, in the order I'd use them. Each one teaches you something real, and each demonstrates you understand his world rather than testing whether he has a problem.

Open with his own post: *you wrote that we're delegating to agents now and the question is intent versus orders — in practice, where does authority actually stop today? What can an agent do at Trendyol without a human in the loop?* His answer is the gap, described by him, which is infinitely better than you asserting it.

Then the thesis, asked rather than argued: *who owns agent infrastructure across teams — is there a platform team for it yet, or is each team rolling its own?* If he says each team, you've won the argument without making it. If he says there is one, you've just found the actual buyer.

Then get the objection out early, while you can still handle it: *what's the thing that would make you say no to an agent going near production data?* Far better to hear it at minute eight than to trip on it at minute twenty.

Then the one senior people rarely get asked: *of the AI work you rolled out, what didn't stick, and why?* His talk covers cultural resistance; he'll have a real answer and he'll respect the question more than "what worked."

And the most tactically valuable one, which tells him nothing and tells you everything: *if an engineer here wanted to try something like this internally, what's the actual path — does that need approval, or can they just do it?* His answer tells you whether your ask is even feasible **before** you make it. Ask this at around minute twenty and shape the close around what he says.

Don't ask about budget. Don't ask whether he has the problem — leading questions read as sales. And don't ask him to walk you through their fraud architecture; an outsider probing that is a bad look regardless of intent.

## What success looks like at 14:30

A named engineer, a named slice of work, and a date before Umut's 1-1 on the 24th. That's it. If you leave with that, this was a good meeting even if he never says a warm word.

If you leave with "let's stay in touch and I'm happy to advise," you got the consolation prize. Push once before you accept it — *would it be easier if Umut just spiked something small and showed you on the 24th?*

---

**Confidence**

- The positioning: **high** that it's the right frame for him — it's derived from his own published words, not from generic enterprise pitch logic.
- The goal recommendation: **medium-high**. It follows from your constraints and where you actually are, but it's my judgment call about what's worth more, and reasonable people would argue for taking the advisor relationship as a foothold. I don't think that's right for you now, and I'd rather say so plainly than list options.
- The questions: judgment, tested only against what he's written publicly.
- Unchanged and still the biggest unknown: whether the fraud work is his. Question two above partly covers you either way.

**Next actions**

1. Let me write the opening and the Marquet bridge out in full, Turkish and English, so you can pick in the room.
2. I can put the five questions on one page in the order above — something you can glance at without reading.
3. Decide now, before the call, that advisor is not the outcome you're optimizing for. That decision is much harder to make live.
4. Message Umut.

content.text:
You're right, and that was bad advice. Umut introduced you as someone with a product — Yiğit turned up to see it. Opening with a five-question battery makes him do the work and reads as a discovery call. Scrap that.

## Show first, ask second

With a technical peer, the artifact generates the conversation. Once he's seen it, what he pokes at *is* your discovery — and it's better than anything he'd say to a survey. You also can't fix "I struggle to explain the product" by avoiding explaining it. This is the rep.

**0–2 min.** Thank him, name Umut, then say what it is in two sentences and stop. No preamble about the journey.

**2–10 min.** Show it. Early, while attention is highest. One artifact, the one you're most fluent in. Say the Marquet line as the *reason it's built this way*, not as a question — you're delegating to agents now, intent not orders, and the mechanics of that are permissions, approvals, and a record of what happened. Then show that.

**10–25 min.** He'll interrupt. That's the meeting. An ex-founder who runs 750 engineers will push on isolation, on data residency, on why not n8n, on why not build it. Every one of those is worth more than a question you'd have asked. Answer straight, concede what's true, don't defend.

**25–30 min.** The ask and a date.

## Keep two questions, not five

Have them in your pocket for when the conversation opens naturally, not as a list you work through.

The one you genuinely need: **who owns agent infrastructure across teams — a platform team, or is each team rolling its own?** That's your entire thesis, and his answer either hands you the argument or hands you the buyer.

The one that shapes your close: **if an engineer here wanted to try something like this internally, what's the actual path?** Ask it around minute twenty-two. His answer tells you whether the Umut spike is a five-minute yes or needs security review — and you shape the ask accordingly instead of guessing.

Everything else I listed is optional. If the conversation goes there, good. If not, you lose nothing.

## The one thing to protect

Don't let the demo run past ten minutes. The failure mode for a founder who's nervous about explaining the product is filling silence with more product. Show one thing, stop talking, let him react. The silence after you stop is where the meeting actually happens.

---

**Confidence:** medium-high on the revised shape — it fits how the intro was framed and who he is. The two questions are the ones I'd bet on; the rest was me over-applying discovery-call logic to a peer conversation that isn't one.

**Next actions**

1. Let me write the two opening sentences — that's now the highest-value thing on the list, since everything hinges on the first two minutes.
2. Pick your one demo now and run it once end to end so it's muscle memory.
3. Decide the exact ask sentence, so you're not composing it at minute 26.
4. Umut.

content.text:
## Marquet

David Marquet — US Navy captain who took command of the USS Santa Fe, a nuclear submarine that was the worst-performing in its fleet, and turned it into one of the best inside a year. He wrote it up as *Turn the Ship Around!*

The pivotal moment: he'd trained for a whole year on a different submarine and got reassigned at the last minute, so he didn't actually know this boat. One day he gave an order that was impossible on that particular ship — and the crew tried to carry it out anyway. He asked why nobody objected. The answer was one line: **"Because you said so."** He realized he was commanding a culture of yes-men, which on a nuclear submarine isn't just inefficient, it's dangerous.

His fix was a language change. Navy convention is "I request permission to submerge." He banned it and replaced it with **"I intend to submerge."** The point being that to say "I intend," you must already have thought through every justification: *Captain, I intend to submerge. We're in our own waters, depth checked at 400 feet, all personnel below, ship ready to dive.* Captain says "very well." The authority still sits with him — but the thinking has moved down to where the information is.

Marquet's compressed version, which is the line Yiğit quotes: **don't move information up to authority; move authority down to where the information is.** With the caveat that delegated authority alone isn't enough — it needs competence (so delegating is safe) and clarity (so everyone knows the intent). Without all three, "I trust you" just pushes people into a void.

**And here's why it matters for you:** Yiğit wrote all of that on LinkedIn four weeks ago, in Turkish, and then closed the post by extending it to AI — *we're now delegating not only to people but to agents; the question is the same, orders or intent.*

So the opening isn't you citing a management book. It's you saying **"I read your post."** Don't pretend to have read Marquet — if he asks, you've read his post about it, which is true and is the better answer anyway. Referencing someone's own writing beats referencing their favourite author every time.

## On the demo

Good pick, and it's the one that fits every opening. Two things it demands: rehearse the happy path until it's boring, and make the action look real rather than a toy — an agent trying to do something with consequences, hitting the approval, a human deciding, and the whole thing recorded. That sequence *is* "intent not orders" made concrete, which is why it works no matter which opening you choose.

Now that Marquet makes sense, pick the opening.

# Yiğit Darçın — Mon 17 Aug, 14:00–14:30 BST (16:00 Istanbul)

meet.google.com/yqy-pivp-scx · 30 min

**Him:** Director of Engineering, Trendyol Group (Umut calls him VP of Eng — don't use a title).
Leads data, ML, core tech — 750+ of Trendyol's ~2,000 engineers. Ex co-founder of Dolap (acquired
by Trendyol). n11, Turkcell before. Bilkent CS. 20+ yrs.

**How you got here:** You asked Umut on 11 Aug. He emailed the intro on 14 Aug
("Tanistirma: Emre x Yigit" — in emre@lobu.ai, read it). He booked himself.
**Umut has a 1-1 with him on 24 Aug** — that's your second touch, design for it.

---

## Open (0–2 min)

> "Umut mentioned your teams are delegating real work to agents now. I read your post on
> Turn the Ship Around — the line about moving authority to where the information is, rather
> than moving information up to authority.
>
> That's basically what I've been building for agents: what it can see, what it can do without
> asking, and what it actually did. Open source, runs on your infra."

If he looks blank: *"you ended it saying we delegate to agents now too — orders or intent."*

You read **his post**, not the book. That's true, and it's the better answer.

## Demo (2–10 min) — approvals / delegation

Agent attempts a real action → approval card → human decides → run + provenance recorded.
That sequence IS the opening sentence, live.

Rehearse the happy path until it's boring. Make the action look consequential, not a toy.
**Stop at ten minutes.** The silence after you stop is where the meeting happens.

## Then shut up (10–25 min)

He'll push on isolation, data residency, why not n8n, why not build it. That's the discovery.
Answer straight, concede what's true, don't defend.

Two questions in your pocket — deploy when natural, not as a list:

1. Who owns agent infrastructure across teams — a platform team, or each team rolling its own?
2. (~min 22) If an engineer here wanted to try something like this internally, what's the actual path?

Q2 tells you whether your ask is a five-minute yes or needs security review. Ask before you ask.

## Ask (25–30 min) — laddered

**Floor:** let Umut spike it. Costs nothing, no procurement, no data access, and he reports back
on the 24th anyway.

**Only if he leans in:** "the way I work with early teams is I sit with them a couple of weeks and
build the first thing with them." His own talk is called *AI in the trenches* — that phrasing lands.

**Never frame it as availability.** Umut is his direct report; "I'd like to be embedded" can read
as a backdoor job approach.

**Close on:** a named engineer + a named slice + a date before 24 Aug.

---

## Objections

- *"We'll just build it."* → Agree. It's open source, read every line. The part not worth building
  six times is isolation/approval/audit, not the agent loop.
- *"Where does our data go?"* → Your infra, full stop. Lead with this, don't wait to be asked.
- *"Why not n8n?"* → n8n is stateless workflow glue with credentials sitting in the workflow.
  Lobu is stateful and permission-aware, secrets the runtime never sees.
- *Isolation probe* → org/agent boundary, workers see `lobu_secret_<uuid>` placeholders,
  cross-org runs rejected. **Not** per-employee. Don't stretch it.

## Do not

- Claim per-employee isolation.
- Claim any fraud domain expertise. You don't have it; he does.
- Bring KPIs. He cites **Goodhart's Law** — a measure that becomes a target stops being a good
  measure. Talk system and behaviour; let numbers be a consequence.
- Accept "happy to advise" as the outcome. Push once: *"would it be easier if Umut just spiked
  something small and showed you on the 24th?"*
- Let the demo run long.

## Him, in his own words (last ~8 months)

- **4wk ago** — Marquet / *Turn the Ship Around*: authority to where the information is; needs
  competence + clarity too. Closes on delegating to **agents**: orders or intent?
- **1mo** — Bill Walsh, *The Score Takes Care of Itself*: don't set the number, build the system.
  Cites Goodhart. Character over talent in hiring.
- **1mo** — Green Book / anti-multitasking: few things, finished, closed. **Don't propose a big
  parallel initiative.**
- **Feb (X)** — Chad Fowler's *Relocating Rigor*: "the best transformations don't remove
  discipline — they relocate rigor closer to feedback, tests, and reality."
- **Dec 2025 (X)** — "the ML platform team I'm proud to be part of took ML at Trendyol from
  'individual projects' to a platform."
- **LeadDev talk** — *AI in the trenches: real-world wins without breaking things*. n8n, Cursor,
  A2A, MCPs across 2,000 engineers, +30% delivery. Governance and discipline, not hype.
- Publicly champions Turkish tech (eachlabs, PrimeTek). Reposted Trendyol × Man City 3d ago.

**He already uses MCP.** Skip the explainer.

## Still unknown

Whether the fraud tool is in his org. Umut said 11 Aug, from inside a Trendyol meeting:
*"basic bir fraud toolu yapmak istiyorlar"* + *"bu iş Lobu'da yapılır"*. He never said whose.
**Ask Umut before 14:00.**

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

input.content:
Meeting brief

Intent, Not Orders

Yiğit Darçın — Director of Engineering, Trendyol Group. Data, ML and core technology; 750+ of Trendyol's ~2,000 engineers. Ex co-founder of Dolap. Umut calls him VP of Eng, so don't use a title to his face.

Mon 17 Aug · 14:00–14:30 BST 16:00 Istanbul — meet.google.com/yqy-pivp-scx

Say this first

“Umut mentioned your teams are delegating real work to agents now. I read your post on Turn the Ship Around — the line about moving authority to where the information is, rather than moving information up to authority.

That's basically what I've been building for agents: what it can see, what it can do without asking, and what it actually did. Open source, runs on your infra.”

If he looks blank: “you ended it saying we delegate to agents now too — orders or intent.” You read his post, not the book. That's true, and it's the better answer.

The thirty minutes

00–02

Open, then stop

Thank him, name Umut, say the two sentences above. No preamble about the journey. Don't explain the company.

02–10

Demo — approvals and delegation

Agent attempts a real action → approval card → human decides → run and provenance recorded. That sequence is the opening sentence, live.

Rehearse the happy path until it's boring. Make the action look consequential, not a toy. Stop at ten minutes.

10–25

Shut up and let him push

He'll go at isolation, data residency, why not n8n, why not build it. That's the discovery — better than anything you'd have asked. Answer straight, concede what's true, don't defend. The silence after you stop talking is where the meeting happens.

25–30

Ask, and put a date on it

Named engineer, named slice of work, a date before 24 August — the day Umut has his 1-1 with him.

Two questions, in your pocket

Not a list you work through. Deploy them when the conversation opens naturally.

Who owns agent infrastructure across teams — a platform team, or is each team rolling its own?

If each team: you've won the argument without making it. If there's a platform team: you've just found the buyer.

If an engineer here wanted to try something like this internally, what's the actual path?

Ask around minute 22. Tells you whether your ask is a five-minute yes or needs security review — before you make it.

The ask

Floor — ask for this

Let Umut spike it. No procurement, no legal, no data access, and he reports back on the 24th anyway. Hard to refuse.

Only if he leans in

“The way I work with early teams is I sit with them a couple of weeks and build the first thing with them.” His own talk is called AI in the trenches — that phrasing lands.

Never frame it as

Availability. Umut is his direct report; “I'd like to be embedded” can read as a backdoor job approach. Always: how you work with early customers.

Objections

“We'll just build it.”

Agree. It's open source, read every line. The part not worth building six times is isolation, approval and audit — not the agent loop.

“Where does our data go?”

Your infra, full stop. Lead with this; don't wait to be asked.

“Why not n8n?”

n8n is stateless workflow glue with credentials sitting in the workflow. Lobu is stateful and permission-aware, with secrets the runtime never sees.

Isolation probe

Org and agent boundary, workers see lobu_secret_<uuid> placeholders, cross-org runs rejected. Not per-employee. Don't stretch it.

Do not

  • Claim per-employee isolation.
  • Claim fraud domain expertise. You don't have it; he does.
  • Bring KPIs. He cites Goodhart's Law — a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure. Talk system and behaviour; let numbers be a consequence.
  • Propose a big parallel initiative. He posted a plea against multitasking last month: few things, finished, closed.
  • Accept “happy to advise” as the outcome. Push once: “would it be easier if Umut just spiked something small and showed you on the 24th?”
  • Let the demo run long.

Him, in his own words

4 wks ago
Marquet, Turn the Ship Around. Authority to where the information is — but it needs competence and clarity too. Closes on delegating to agents: orders or intent?
1 mo
Bill Walsh, The Score Takes Care of Itself. Don't set the number, build the system that produces it. Cites Goodhart. Character over talent in hiring.
1 mo
Green Book / anti-multitasking. Few things, finished, closed. Don't pile parallel work on teams.
Feb · X
Chad Fowler's Relocating Rigor — “the best transformations don't remove discipline, they relocate rigor closer to feedback, tests, and reality.”
Dec 2025 · X
“The ML platform team I'm proud to be part of took ML at Trendyol from individual projects to a platform.”
LeadDev
AI in the trenches: real-world wins without breaking things. n8n, Cursor, A2A and MCPs across 2,000 engineers, +30% delivery speed. Governance and discipline, not hype. He already uses MCP — skip the explainer.
Ongoing
Publicly champions Turkish tech — eachlabs, PrimeTek. Reposted the Trendyol × Manchester City partnership three days ago, if you need thirty seconds of warm-up.

Still unknown

Whether the fraud tool is in his org. Umut wrote on 11 August, from inside a Trendyol meeting: “basic bir fraud toolu yapmak istiyorlar” and “bu iş Lobu'da yapılır.” He never said whose project it is.

Ask Umut before 14:00. It's one line, and it decides whether fraud is your opening example or a card you keep in your pocket.

# Yiğit Darçın — Mon 17 Aug, 14:00–14:30 BST (16:00 Istanbul)

meet.google.com/yqy-pivp-scx · 30 min

**Him:** Director of Engineering, Trendyol Group (Umut calls him VP of Eng — don't use a title).
Leads data, ML, core tech — 750+ of Trendyol's ~2,000 engineers. Ex co-founder of Dolap (acquired
by Trendyol). n11, Turkcell before. Bilkent CS. 20+ yrs.

**How you got here:** You asked Umut on 11 Aug. He emailed the intro on 14 Aug
("Tanistirma: Emre x Yigit" — in emre@lobu.ai, read it). He booked himself.
**Umut has a 1-1 with him on 24 Aug** — that's your second touch, design for it.

---

## Open (0–2 min)

> "Umut mentioned your teams are delegating real work to agents now. I read your post on
> Turn the Ship Around — the line about moving authority to where the information is, rather
> than moving information up to authority.
>
> That's basically what I've been building for agents: what it can see, what it can do without
> asking, and what it actually did. Open source, runs on your infra."

If he looks blank: *"you ended it saying we delegate to agents now too — orders or intent."*

You read **his post**, not the book. That's true, and it's the better answer.

## Demo (2–10 min) — approvals / delegation

Agent attempts a real action → approval card → human decides → run + provenance recorded.
That sequence IS the opening sentence, live.

Rehearse the happy path until it's boring. Make the action look consequential, not a toy.
**Stop at ten minutes.** The silence after you stop is where the meeting happens.

## Then shut up (10–25 min)

He'll push on isolation, data residency, why not n8n, why not build it. That's the discovery.
Answer straight, concede what's true, don't defend.

Two questions in your pocket — deploy when natural, not as a list:

1. Who owns agent infrastructure across teams — a platform team, or each team rolling its own?
2. (~min 22) If an engineer here wanted to try something like this internally, what's the actual path?

Q2 tells you whether your ask is a five-minute yes or needs security review. Ask before you ask.

## Ask (25–30 min) — laddered

**Floor:** let Umut spike it. Costs nothing, no procurement, no data access, and he reports back
on the 24th anyway.

**Only if he leans in:** "the way I work with early teams is I sit with them a couple of weeks and
build the first thing with them." His own talk is called *AI in the trenches* — that phrasing lands.

**Never frame it as availability.** Umut is his direct report; "I'd like to be embedded" can read
as a backdoor job approach.

**Close on:** a named engineer + a named slice + a date before 24 Aug.

---

## Objections

- *"We'll just build it."* → Agree. It's open source, read every line. The part not worth building
  six times is isolation/approval/audit, not the agent loop.
- *"Where does our data go?"* → Your infra, full stop. Lead with this, don't wait to be asked.
- *"Why not n8n?"* → n8n is stateless workflow glue with credentials sitting in the workflow.
  Lobu is stateful and permission-aware, secrets the runtime never sees.
- *Isolation probe* → org/agent boundary, workers see `lobu_secret_<uuid>` placeholders,
  cross-org runs rejected. **Not** per-employee. Don't stretch it.

## Do not

- Claim per-employee isolation.
- Claim any fraud domain expertise. You don't have it; he does.
- Bring KPIs. He cites **Goodhart's Law** — a measure that becomes a target stops being a good
  measure. Talk system and behaviour; let numbers be a consequence.
- Accept "happy to advise" as the outcome. Push once: *"would it be easier if Umut just spiked
  something small and showed you on the 24th?"*
- Let the demo run long.

  Cites Goodhart. Character over talent in hiring.

  parallel initiative.**
- **Feb (X)** — Chad Fowler's *Relocating Rigor*: "the best transformations don't remove
  discipline — they relocate rigor closer to feedback, tests, and reality."
- **Dec 2025 (X)** — "the ML platform team I'm proud to be part of took ML at Trendyol from
  'individual projects' to a platform."
- **LeadDev talk** — *AI in the trenches: real-world wins without breaking things*. n8n, Cursor,

**He already uses MCP.** Skip the explainer.

## Still unknown

Whether the fraud tool is in his org. Umut said 11 Aug, from inside a Trendyol meeting:
*"basic bir fraud toolu yapmak istiyorlar"* + *"bu iş Lobu'da yapılır"*. He never said whose.

<!-- Rules for agents (Claude, pi, codex); CLAUDE.md inlines this into every session. Keep it to facts an agent cannot derive and boundaries it must not cross. Reasoning and recipes go in docs/AGENT_PLAYBOOK.md, package specifics in the nearest package AGENTS.md. -->

## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it. For a pure submodule-pointer bump, `make bump SUBMODULE=packages/owletto` is the lightweight isolated-worktree exception; it also posts the required statuses.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup` (only task-setup does submodule pinning, `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation); only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.
- **Never auto-submit an interactive browser draft, in any package.** Drafts are page-activated: persist the operation, notify normally, and let the extension activate the run only when the user visits a pending URL in a user-owned tab. Only scrape-owned scratch tabs may be opened and closed automatically. Server, connector, and Owletto code all obey this (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`).

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `automations`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **Automation is the product, API, and storage vocabulary.** Use it consistently in public contracts and internal identifiers; `make pre-pr-remote` rejects retired product and engine terminology.
- **`make review` is the semantic review gate, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; a verdict or safe-class skip is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new production dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment. Tests may import dynamically after mocks; two Node-version gates are grandfathered (playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. Safe-class changes self-skip before selecting an LLM. Otherwise it runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status. Narrow path/content-gated safe classes skip the cross-harness review; this includes pure `packages/owletto` pointer bumps and exact `model:` literal swaps, but not mixed runtime and source changes. The submodule's own repo owns its content review.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes and complete, forward-only Owletto pointer diffs confined to `deploy/` pass as not applicable; other pointer changes need exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; see the playbook).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported. Lobu's required `integration` fan-in is absent from `gh pr checks` until it starts, not pending, so diff against the branch-protection list (playbook).
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

## How to work
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- **Evidence, not assertion.** Never report done off a green typecheck — boot it, exercise every branch you touched, and clean up test data; if "compiles" is all you ran, say so. Show `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`, including for a dispatched agent's work.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`:** `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`. A working-tree grep proves nothing, and the fetch is load-bearing.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence — a dangling import, a completed migration, a superseded implementation. Low prod usage is not evidence, and docs and help text are load-bearing.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other occurrence and fix in one pass. A diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one.
- One branch = one concern. Never `git stash`; use WIP commits.
- Prefer `bun`, never npm/yarn/pnpm. Before adding an env var, grep for the one already read, and do not rename existing vars unasked.
- Block only on irreversible or destructive actions and decisions genuinely the user's; otherwise take the recommended option and flag it in your summary.
- Never poll in the foreground — run long waits in the background and act on the notification. Poll delegated CLIs at most once every 4.5 minutes unless they finish or request input.
- Prefer DOM reads over screenshots, the top context-bloat source. The paired Owletto extension drives the user's real logged-in browser; CDP is not required (`docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`).
- Slack link pasted → run `scripts/slack-thread-viewer.js "<link>"` first.
- `make dev-remote` runs the live app on remote compute (commit first; `make dev-remote-pause` when finished).

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## claude.ai PostHog
# PostHog `exec` covers

action|agent-feedback|alert|annotation|apm|approval|batch-export|cdp-function|channel|cohorts|comment|conversations|dashboard|data-warehouse|docs-search|early-access-feature|endpoint|error-tracking|event-definition|execute-sql|experiment|experiment-activity|experiment-archive|experiment-calculate|experiment-copy|experiment-duplicate|experiment-end|experiment-freeze|experiment-launch|experiment-metrics|experiment-pause|experiment-prompt|experiment-reset|experiment-results|experiment-resume|experiment-saved|experiment-ship|experiment-stats|experiment-timeseries|experiment-unarchive|experiment-unfreeze|external-data-schemas|external-data-sources|external-data-sync|feature-flag|file-download-batch|generate-app-url|health-issues|heatmaps|inbox|insight|integration|llm-total-costs|llma-clustering|llma-evaluation|llma-parser|llma-personal|llma-prompt|llma-review|llma-score|llma-skill|llma-summarization|llma-tagger|llma-trace|logs|marketing-analytics|mcp|notebooks|opt-outs|org-member|organization|path-cleaning-rules|persons|project|proxy|query|read-data-schema|reminder|role|saved-query-column|scheduled-changes|scout|session-recording|signals-scout|skill|sql-variables|subscriptions|survey|switch|usage-metrics|user|view|vision|warehouse|web-analytics-weekly|workflows|workflows-archive|workflows-blast|workflows-discard|workflows-enable|workflows-global|workflows-logs|workflows-patch|workflows-publish|workflows-restore|workflows-schedule|workflows-show|workflows-stats|workflows-test

# Tools

exec – run any PostHog command; its `command` description has the syntax.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors.
